nameStory: This western wanderer is named after John Cassin, a 19th-century American ornithologist who described many bird species from specimens brought back by western expeditions. Like other kingbirds, it earns the 'king' part of its name through its bold, aggressive behavior toward much larger birds that dare enter its territory.
description: Cassin's Kingbird is a sturdy, medium-sized flycatcher about the size of a robin, with a big head and broad shoulders that give it a confident posture. This western species sports dark gray upperparts and a white throat that contrasts sharply with its darker chest. Though native to western North America, a few adventurous individuals occasionally wander into New England, making any sighting here a special treat for birders. Like other flycatchers, it catches insects on the wing with impressive aerial acrobatics.

idTips.label: White throat patch
idTips.description: Look for a bright white throat that stands out like a bib against the dark gray chest and head - this clean contrast is striking and visible even from a distance

idTips.label: Dark gray upperparts
idTips.description: The back, wings, and head appear charcoal gray, giving the bird a somewhat somber, dignified appearance compared to other kingbirds

idTips.label: Square-tipped tail
idTips.description: The tail appears cut straight across when spread, lacking the forked or notched shape of some similar species

idTips.label: Upright perching posture
idTips.description: Sits bolt upright on exposed perches like fence posts or dead branches, chest puffed out like a proud sentinel surveying its domain

idTips.label: Large head and bill
idTips.description: The head looks oversized for the body, with a thick, sturdy bill perfect for catching flying insects with a satisfying snap

habitat: In New England, any Cassin's Kingbird would be a rare vagrant found in open areas like fields, parks, or coastal areas with scattered trees for perching. Look for them on prominent perches like fence posts, telephone wires, or isolated dead branches where they can scan for flying insects. They prefer edge habitats where open ground meets scattered trees or shrubs.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare vagrant that might appear during spring migration, typically found in open areas actively hawking insects from prominent perches.
seasonality.summer: Any summer sightings would be exceptional vagrants, likely maintaining typical flycatcher behavior of sallying out from perches to catch insects.
seasonality.fall: Most likely season for vagrant appearances during fall migration, when western birds sometimes wander eastward off their normal routes.
seasonality.winter: Essentially absent from New England in winter, as these birds migrate to warmer climates in Mexico and Central America.

funFact: Despite being fierce defenders of their territory who will boldly chase away hawks and eagles many times their size, Cassin's Kingbirds have only been spotted in New England a mere 6 times - making each sighting rarer than finding a four-leaf clover!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Eastern Kingbird, but Cassin's has a white throat contrasting with gray chest (Eastern has white underparts), and lacks Eastern's distinctive white tail band. Think 'Cassin's = Contrast' between the white throat and gray body to remember the key difference.
contextualKnowledge: Cassin's Kingbird sightings in New England are so rare they're considered 'mega-rarities' that draw birders from across the region. Any potential sighting should be carefully documented and reported to eBird, as it would represent a significant vagrant record for the area.
compareHints: Unlike the familiar Eastern Kingbird with its clean white underparts and white-tipped tail, Cassin's Kingbird shows the distinctive white throat against gray chest pattern. Western Kingbird is more similar but has yellow on the belly and white outer tail feathers, while Cassin's lacks both features and appears more uniformly gray overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eastern Kingbirds are the only kingbird species that regularly breeds in New England, making identification easier than in western regions where multiple kingbird species overlap.
Western Kingbirds are easily distinguished from their Eastern Kingbird cousins by their bright yellow underparts versus the Eastern's clean white belly.

Among its kingbird relatives, the Scissor-tailed Flycatcher is instantly distinguished by its extraordinarily long, forked tail - Eastern Kingbirds have much shorter, square tails with white tips, while Western Kingbirds have moderately long tails but nothing approaching the dramatic streamers of the Scissor-tailed.
Among the kingbirds, Tropical Kingbird's bright yellow belly immediately separates it from the white-bellied Eastern Kingbird.
Unlike its kingbird relatives, the Fork-tailed Flycatcher has that unmistakable extremely long, forked tail that no other kingbird possesses.
Unlike Eastern Kingbirds with their stark black caps and white tail bands, Gray Kingbirds are much more subtly colored in pale gray and white.
